records.source: אֵיכָ֣ה׀יָשְׁבָ֣ה בָדָ֗ד הָעִיר֙ רַבָּ֣תִי עָ֔ם הָיְתָ֖ה כְּאַלְמָנָ֑ה רַּבָּ֣תִיבַגּוֹיִ֗ם שָׂרָ֨תִי֙ בַּמְּדִינ֔וֹת הָיְתָ֖ה לָמַֽס׃ס
records.gloss: How sits alone the city great of people! She has become like a widow, great among [the] nations; princess among [the] provinces, she has become forced labor.
pieces: How the city sits alone that once was crowded with people! \q She has become like a widow, \q she who was great among the nations; \q the princess of the provinces is now put to forced labor.

L.1: How she sits alone, the city [once] great with people! \q She has become like a widow, \q she [who was] great among the nations; \q [the] princess among the provinces has become a forced laborer.

R.1: How lonely the city is now, the city that was once full of people! \q Now she is like a widow, \q though she was great among the nations. \q She was a princess over other lands, but now she must do forced labor.

decisions.choice: an alphabet poem: twenty-two verses, one for each letter
decisions.reason: This chapter is an acrostic. Each of its twenty-two verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet in order: this verse with aleph, verse 2 with beth, and so on to taw in verse 22. Chapters 2 and 4 follow the same plan, chapter 3 gives each letter three verses, and chapter 5 has twenty-two verses but does not follow the alphabet. The form gives grief an order and a fullness, from the first letter to the last.

decisions.choice: How ...!: a cry of grief and shock, and the book's Hebrew title
decisions.reason: The word ('ekhah) is an exclamation, not a question: the cry of a mourner over the dead (compare Isaiah 1:21; Jeremiah 48:17), here over a fallen city. It opens chapters 1, 2 and 4, and it is the Hebrew name of the book.

decisions.choice: the lament rhythm: verses of three lines, each line long then short
decisions.reason: Most verses of this chapter have three lines (verse 7 has four). Many lines fall into a longer and a shorter half, a limping beat that was used for funeral songs (qinah, 2 Samuel 1:17; Amos 5:1-2). The Hebrew accents divide each verse in two, and the lines here follow those divisions.

decisions.choice: like a widow: bereft of husband and protector
decisions.reason: A widow had lost the one who provided for her and spoke for her, and she was easily wronged (Exodus 22:21; Isaiah 54:4). The city that was full of people now sits alone, emptied of her people and her king. The word "like" keeps it a picture: the city is not said to have lost her God for good.

decisions.choice: forced labor: work exacted by a ruling power
decisions.reason: The word (mas) names the labor gangs a ruler imposed on a subject people. Israel once put the Canaanites to such labor (Joshua 16:10; 1 Kings 9:21); now the princess among the provinces is the one made to serve. The reversal runs through the chapter.

decisions.choice: How ...!
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "How" with an exclamation mark, since the word is a cry, not a request for information, and it is the name of the book (m2). Chapters 2 and 4 open the same way.

decisions.choice: lonely ... now ... though ... over other lands
decisions.reason: Readable makes the contrast between then and now plain with "now" and "though", and says "other lands" for the provinces, the districts of an empire.

records.heading: The city sits alone

records.source: בָּכ֨וֹ תִבְכֶּ֜ה בַּלַּ֗יְלָה וְדִמְעָתָהּ֙ עַ֣ל לֶֽחֱיָ֔הּ אֵֽין־לָ֥הּ מְנַחֵ֖ם מִכָּל־אֹהֲבֶ֑יהָ כָּל־רֵעֶ֨יהָ֙ בָּ֣גְדוּ בָ֔הּ הָ֥יוּ לָ֖הּ לְאֹיְבִֽים׃ס
records.gloss: Weeping she weeps in the night, and her tear[s] [are] on her cheek; there is not for her a comforter from all her lovers; all her friends have dealt treacherously with her, they have become to her enemies.
pieces: Bitterly she weeps through the night, with tears on her cheeks; \q of all her lovers there is not one to comfort her; \q all her friends have betrayed her and turned into her enemies.

L.2: She weeps and weeps in the night, and her tears [are] on her cheek; \q she has no comforter among all her lovers; \q all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.

R.2: She cries and cries all night long, with tears running down her face. \q She had many lovers, but none of them comforts her now. \q All her friends have turned against her and become her enemies.

decisions.choice: weeping she weeps: she weeps without stopping
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled, a Hebrew way of making it strong: she weeps hard and long. "In the night" adds that her grief gives her no rest when others sleep.

decisions.choice: her lovers, her friends: the nations she trusted as allies
decisions.reason: The city is pictured as a woman who turned from her husband to lovers. The prophets use this picture for Judah's alliances with other nations and the trust she put in them and in their gods (Jeremiah 4:30; 22:20-22; 30:14). Those allies did nothing for her, and some joined her enemies.

decisions.choice: comforter: one who comes to console a mourner
decisions.reason: A comforter was the friend or relative who came to sit with someone in grief (Genesis 37:35; Job 2:11). "No one to comfort her" returns again and again in this chapter (verses 9, 16, 17, 21).

decisions.choice: Bitterly she weeps (Balanced); She cries and cries (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the force of the doubled verb with "bitterly", Readable by repeating the verb (m1).

records.source: גָּֽלְתָ֨ה יְהוּדָ֤ה מֵעֹ֨נִי֙ וּמֵרֹ֣ב עֲבֹדָ֔ה הִ֚יא יָשְׁבָ֣ה בַגּוֹיִ֔ם לֹ֥א מָצְאָ֖ה מָנ֑וֹחַ כָּל־רֹדְפֶ֥יהָ הִשִּׂיג֖וּהָ בֵּ֥ין הַמְּצָרִֽים׃ס
records.gloss: Has gone into exile Judah from affliction and from greatness of servitude; she dwells among the nations, not she has found a resting place; all her pursuers have overtaken her between the narrow places.
pieces: Judah has gone into exile after misery and hard servitude; \q she lives among the nations and finds no place to rest; \q all who chased her have caught her in the narrow passes.

L.3: Judah has gone into exile from affliction and from great servitude; \q she dwells among the nations, she has found no resting place; \q all her pursuers have overtaken her between the narrow places.

R.3: Judah has been taken away into exile after suffering and cruel, hard work. \q She lives among the nations and finds no place to rest. \q Everyone who chased her has caught her where she could not escape.

decisions.choice: from affliction: after a time of suffering and servitude
decisions.reason: The small word "from" can mean "after" or "because of". Read as "after", Judah's exile came on top of years of suffering under foreign powers. Read as "because of", some of Judah's people left the land to escape that suffering. The first fits the chapter, where exile is the last of her losses.

decisions.choice: she has found no resting place: the curse of Deuteronomy come true
decisions.reason: Moses warned that if Israel broke the covenant, "among those nations you will find no rest, no resting place for the sole of your foot" (Deuteronomy 28:64-65). The same word for a resting place is used there.

decisions.choice: between the narrow places: trapped with no way out
decisions.reason: The word is used of a narrow pass between rocks, a place where those being chased are caught. It also stands for distress in general (Psalm 116:3). Judah was overtaken like someone run down in a ravine. Judah's king was caught as he fled (2 Kings 25:4-5).

decisions.choice: where she could not escape
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the narrow places (m3).

records.source: דַּרְכֵ֨י צִיּ֜וֹן אֲבֵל֗וֹת מִבְּלִי֙ בָּאֵ֣י מוֹעֵ֔ד כָּל־שְׁעָרֶ֨יהָ֙ שֽׁוֹמֵמִ֔ין כֹּהֲנֶ֖יהָ נֶאֱנָחִ֑ים בְּתוּלֹתֶ֥יהָ נּוּג֖וֹתוְהִ֥יא מַר־לָֽהּ׃ס
records.gloss: [The] roads of Zion [are] mourning from no ones coming [to the] appointed feast; all her gates [are] desolate, her priests [are] groaning; her virgins [are] grieved, and she, bitter to her.
pieces: The roads to Zion mourn, for no one comes to the festivals; \q all her gates are deserted, her priests groan; \q her young women grieve, and she herself is in bitter pain.

L.4: The roads of Zion mourn, because none come to the appointed feast; \q all her gates are desolate, her priests groan; \q her virgins are grieved, and as for her, [it is] bitter to her.

R.4: The roads to Zion are sad and empty, because no one comes to the festivals anymore. \q All her city gates are deserted, and her priests groan. \q Her young women are full of sorrow, and Zion herself is in bitter pain.

decisions.choice: the roads mourn: the empty roads are pictured as mourners
decisions.reason: The roads that once carried crowds of pilgrims lie empty. Like the land in the prophets (Isaiah 24:4; Jeremiah 12:4), they are said to mourn.

decisions.choice: the appointed feast: the yearly pilgrim festivals at the temple
decisions.reason: The word (mo'ed) means an appointed time and so a set festival. Three times a year the people came up to the LORD's house for the great feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16). With the temple burned, no one comes.

decisions.choice: her virgins: the city's young unmarried women
decisions.reason: The word means young women of marriageable age. They led the singing and dancing at festivals and weddings (Judges 21:19-21; Jeremiah 31:13), so their grief marks the end of every celebration.

decisions.choice: are grieved
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is from a root meaning to suffer grief. The ancient Greek translation reads "are led away", which may reflect a slightly different Hebrew word. The Hebrew reading is kept.

decisions.choice: young women
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "young women", which names the same people as the Literal "virgins" (m3).

records.source: הָי֨וּ צָרֶ֤יהָ לְרֹאשׁ֙ אֹיְבֶ֣יהָ שָׁל֔וּ כִּֽי־יְהוָ֥ה הוֹגָ֖הּ עַ֣ל רֹב־פְּשָׁעֶ֑יהָ עוֹלָלֶ֛יהָ הָלְכ֥וּ שְׁבִ֖י לִפְנֵי־צָֽר׃ס
records.gloss: Have become her foes [the] head, her enemies are at ease, for Yahweh has grieved her on [account of the] multitude of her transgressions; her children have gone [into] captivity before [the] foe.
pieces: Her foes have become her masters, her enemies live at ease, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has brought grief on her for her many rebellions; \q her little ones have gone into captivity ahead of the foe.

L.5: Her foes have become the head, her enemies are at ease, \q for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has made her suffer for the multitude of her transgressions; \q her children have gone away captive before the foe.

R.5: Her enemies now rule over her and live in comfort. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has made her suffer because she rebelled against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} so many times. \q Her children have been taken away as prisoners, driven ahead of the enemy.

decisions.choice: her foes have become the head: the curse of Deuteronomy come true
decisions.reason: Moses promised that a faithful Israel would be "the head and not the tail", and warned that if they broke the covenant the foreigner would be the head and they the tail (Deuteronomy 28:13, 44).

decisions.choice: the LORD has made her suffer for her transgressions
decisions.reason: The poet does not see the disaster as chance or as the enemy's work alone. The LORD has brought it, and the cause is her many acts of rebellion against him (verses 8, 14, 18, 22). The word for transgression (pesha') means rebellion, the breaking of faith with a lord.

decisions.choice: her children before the foe: captives driven ahead of their captors
decisions.reason: Prisoners of war were marched in front of the conquering army. The word for children means little ones, too young to fight.

decisions.choice: masters (Balanced); rule over her (Readable); rebellions
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what being "the head" means here (m1), and they say "rebellions" or "rebelled" for the word Literal renders "transgressions" (m2).

decisions.choice: rebelled against him
decisions.reason: Readable names the one she rebelled against, the LORD.

records.source: וַיֵּצֵ֥א מִבַּת־צִיּ֖וֹן כָּל־הֲדָרָ֑הּ הָי֣וּ שָׂרֶ֗יהָ כְּאַיָּלִים֙ לֹא־מָצְא֣וּ מִרְעֶ֔ה וַיֵּלְכ֥וּ בְלֹא־כֹ֖חַ לִפְנֵ֥י רוֹדֵֽף׃ס
records.gloss: And has gone out from [the] daughter of Zion all her splendor; her princes have become like deer [that] not have found pasture, and they have gone without strength before [the] pursuer.
pieces: All her splendor has gone from Daughter Zion; \q her officials are like deer that find no pasture; \q they stumble on without strength ahead of the hunter.

L.6: And from the daughter of Zion all her splendor has departed; \q her princes have become like deer [that] find no pasture, \q and they have gone without strength before the pursuer.

R.6: The people of Zion have lost all their splendor. \q Their leaders are like deer that cannot find any grass to eat. \q They are too weak to get away from the hunter.

decisions.choice: the daughter of Zion: Jerusalem and its people pictured as a young woman
decisions.reason: Zion is the hill of the temple and stands for Jerusalem. "Daughter Zion" pictures the city and its people as a young woman, loved and now shamed (2:1; Isaiah 1:8). The chapter speaks of the city as "she" throughout.

decisions.choice: deer: hunted animals weakened by hunger
decisions.reason: Starved deer cannot outrun the hunter. The ancient Greek translation reads "rams", which needs only different vowels in the Hebrew; the Hebrew reading fits the picture of flight.

decisions.choice: her princes ... before the pursuer: the flight of Judah's leaders
decisions.reason: When the Babylonians broke through the wall, King Zedekiah and his men fled by night and were overtaken near Jericho (2 Kings 25:4-6). The word for princes (sar) means the king's chief men.

decisions.choice: officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The king's chief men (sar) are "princes" at Literal, as in Isaiah and Jeremiah; Balanced and Readable say "officials" and "leaders", since they were not the king's sons.

decisions.choice: the people of Zion ... their
decisions.reason: Readable says "the people of Zion" for "the daughter of Zion", as Isaiah does, and so speaks of "their" splendor and leaders (m1).

records.source: זָֽכְרָ֣ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֗ם יְמֵ֤י עָנְיָהּ֙ וּמְרוּדֶ֔יהָ כֹּ֚ל מַחֲמֻדֶ֔יהָ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָי֖וּ מִ֣ימֵי קֶ֑דֶם בִּנְפֹ֧ל עַמָּ֣הּ בְּיַד־צָ֗ר וְאֵ֤ין עוֹזֵר֙ לָ֔הּ רָא֣וּהָ צָרִ֔ים שָׂחֲק֖וּ עַ֥ל מִשְׁבַּתֶּֽהָ׃ס
records.gloss: Remembers Jerusalem [in the] days of her affliction and her wanderings all her precious things which were from days of antiquity, when fell her people into [the] hand of [a] foe and there was no helper for her; saw her foes, they laughed at her ceasing.
pieces: In the days of her misery and homelessness Jerusalem remembers \q all the treasures that were hers in days gone by. \q When her people fell into the foe's hands and no one came to help her, \q her foes looked on and laughed at her ruin.

L.7: Jerusalem remembers, in the days of her affliction and her wandering, \q all her precious things that were from days of old; \q when her people fell into the hand of the foe, and there was no one to help her, \q the foes saw her; they laughed at her downfall.

R.7: Now Jerusalem suffers and has no home, and she remembers \q all the good things she had long ago. \q Her people fell into the power of the enemy, and no one helped her. \q Her enemies saw her and laughed because she was ruined.

decisions.choice: a verse of four lines
decisions.reason: This verse has four lines where the others in the chapter have three. Some think one of the middle lines was added as an explanation, but the Hebrew text has all four, and they are kept.

decisions.choice: her wandering: her homelessness
decisions.reason: The word means restless wandering, the state of someone with no home (Isaiah 58:7; Lamentations 3:19). Jerusalem's people have been driven from their houses.

decisions.choice: her precious things: everything she treasured
decisions.reason: The word means things that are desired or loved. Here it covers all the city's good things, its wealth and its people, which she remembers in her loss (compare verses 10-11).

decisions.choice: her downfall: her coming to an end
decisions.reason: This word is found only here. It comes from the verb "to cease" or "to stop", the same root as the word for the Sabbath. The foes laugh because she is finished.

decisions.choice: Now Jerusalem suffers and has no home, and she remembers
decisions.reason: Readable turns the phrase "in the days of her affliction and her wandering" into its own clause.

records.source: חֵ֤טְא חָֽטְאָה֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם עַל־כֵּ֖ן לְנִידָ֣ה הָיָ֑תָה כָּֽל־מְכַבְּדֶ֤יהָ הִזִּיל֨וּהָ֙ כִּי־רָא֣וּ עֶרְוָתָ֔הּ גַּם־הִ֥יא נֶאֶנְחָ֖ה וַתָּ֥שָׁב אָחֽוֹר׃ס
records.gloss: Sin has sinned Jerusalem; therefore an impure thing she has become; all [who] honored her despise her, for they have seen her nakedness; also she groans and has turned backward.
pieces: Jerusalem has sinned greatly, and so she has become unclean; \q all who honored her despise her, for they have seen her naked; \q she herself groans and turns her face away.

L.8: Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become an impure thing; \q all who honored her despise her, for they have seen her nakedness; \q she herself also groans and turns backward.

R.8: Jerusalem sinned terribly, so she became unclean. \q Those who used to respect her now look down on her, because they have seen her naked and ashamed. \q She groans and turns away.

decisions.choice: has sinned a sin: has sinned greatly
decisions.reason: The noun and verb from the same root strengthen each other: her sin was grave. Verse 20 doubles a verb in the same way ("I have been very rebellious").

decisions.choice: an impure thing: something unclean that others keep away from
decisions.reason: The word is spelled with an extra letter compared with the word for impurity in verse 17 (niddah). It may be another spelling of that word, or it may come from a verb meaning to shake the head or to wander, giving "an object of scorn" or "a homeless wanderer". Her nakedness here and the uncleanness on her skirts in verse 9 favor impurity.

decisions.choice: impurity: the picture of a woman made unclean by her monthly bleeding
decisions.reason: Under the law, a woman's monthly bleeding made her ritually unclean and kept her apart from others for a time (Leviticus 15:19-24). Being unclean in this way was not a sin, but the prophets used it as a picture of defilement that makes others draw back (Ezekiel 36:17). Jerusalem is shunned like that.

decisions.choice: they have seen her nakedness: she is publicly shamed
decisions.reason: To be stripped and seen naked was the deepest disgrace. The prophets picture the punishment of a city that was unfaithful in this way (Isaiah 47:3; Ezekiel 16:37; Nahum 3:5).

decisions.choice: unclean (Balanced, Readable); turns her face away (Balanced)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "unclean", the word used in the laws of purity. Balanced shows that she turns away in shame.

decisions.choice: naked and ashamed
decisions.reason: Readable adds "ashamed" to say what being seen naked meant (m4).

records.source: טֻמְאָתָ֣הּ בְּשׁוּלֶ֗יהָ לֹ֤א זָֽכְרָה֙ אַחֲרִיתָ֔הּ וַתֵּ֣רֶד פְּלָאִ֔ים אֵ֥ין מְנַחֵ֖ם לָ֑הּ רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ אֶת־עָנְיִ֔י כִּ֥י הִגְדִּ֖יל אוֹיֵֽב׃ס
records.gloss: Her uncleanness [was] in her skirts; not she remembered her end; and she has come down wondrously; there is not a comforter for her. See, Yahweh, my affliction, for has magnified himself [the] enemy!
pieces: Her skirts are stained with her uncleanness; she gave no thought to where she was heading; \q her fall has been beyond belief, and there is no one to comfort her. \q Look, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, at my misery, for the enemy has triumphed!

L.9: Her uncleanness [is] in her skirts; she did not remember her end; \q and she has come down astonishingly; she has no comforter. \q See, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, my affliction, for the enemy has made himself great!

R.9: Her clothes were stained with her uncleanness. She did not think about what would happen to her. \q Her fall was shocking, and no one comforts her. \q Zion cries: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, see how I suffer! My enemy has won!

decisions.choice: her uncleanness in her skirts: a stain she cannot hide
decisions.reason: The picture goes on from verse 8: the blood of a woman's monthly bleeding has stained the hem of her dress, so her uncleanness is plain to everyone (Leviticus 15:19-24). It stands for Jerusalem's sin, now exposed to all.

decisions.choice: she did not remember her end: she gave no thought to where her way would lead
decisions.reason: Her "end" is what would come of her conduct. Moses said of Israel, "If they were wise, they would understand their end" (Deuteronomy 32:29), and Babylon is charged in the same words (Isaiah 47:7).

decisions.choice: See, LORD, my affliction: Zion speaks for the first time
decisions.reason: Up to here the poet has spoken about the city. Now, without any word to introduce her, Zion herself cries out to the LORD in the first person ("my affliction"). The poet's voice returns in verses 10-11, and from verse 11c Zion speaks to the end of the chapter, apart from verse 17. Her words are not set off as a quotation.

decisions.choice: the enemy has made himself great: he boasts in his victory
decisions.reason: The verb means to make oneself great, to act with arrogance over a fallen enemy (Psalm 35:26; Jeremiah 48:26).

decisions.choice: Zion cries:
decisions.reason: Readable says who is now speaking, since the Hebrew changes voice without warning (m3).

records.source: יָדוֹ֙ פָּ֣רַשׂ צָ֔ר עַ֖ל כָּל־מַחֲמַדֶּ֑יהָ כִּֽי־רָאֲתָ֤ה גוֹיִם֙ בָּ֣אוּ מִקְדָּשָׁ֔הּ אֲשֶׁ֣ר צִוִּ֔יתָה לֹא־יָבֹ֥אוּ בַקָּהָ֖ל לָֽךְ׃ס
records.gloss: His hand has spread out [the] foe over all her desirable things; for she has seen nations, they have entered her sanctuary, whom you commanded [that] not they should enter into [the] assembly of yours.
pieces: The foe has reached out his hand for all her treasures; \q she has watched the nations enter her sanctuary, \q the very ones {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} forbade to enter {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} assembly.

L.10: The foe has spread out his hand over all her precious things; \q for she has seen nations enter her sanctuary, \q [those] whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} commanded [that] they should not enter into {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} assembly.

R.10: The enemy has grabbed all her treasures. \q She watched foreign nations go into her temple, \q though {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, had commanded that such people must never join {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} people when they gather.

decisions.choice: her precious things: the treasures of the temple and the city
decisions.reason: The Babylonians carried off the gold, silver and bronze of the LORD's house and the wealth of the palace (2 Kings 24:13; 25:13-17).

decisions.choice: nations whom you commanded not to enter your assembly
decisions.reason: The law kept certain foreign peoples out of "the assembly of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 23:4). Now foreigners have gone further than the assembly: they have walked into the holy place itself, as conquerors.

decisions.choice: you, your: the poet turns to speak to God
decisions.reason: In the middle of describing Zion, the poet addresses God directly: "you commanded". The last word, "your", has an ending that can be read as addressing Zion ("your assembly", hers), but at the end of a verse the same form is used in speaking to a man, and the commandment and the assembly are the LORD's (Deuteronomy 23:4).

decisions.choice: you, LORD ... join your people when they gather
decisions.reason: Readable names the LORD, whom the poet now addresses (m3), and explains the assembly as the gathering of God's people for worship.

records.source: כָּל־עַמָּ֤הּ נֶאֱנָחִים֙ מְבַקְּשִׁ֣ים לֶ֔חֶם נָתְנ֧וּ מַחֲמַדֵּיהֶ֛םבְּאֹ֖כֶל לְהָשִׁ֣יב נָ֑פֶשׁ רְאֵ֤ה יְהוָה֙ וְֽהַבִּ֔יטָה כִּ֥י הָיִ֖יתִי זוֹלֵלָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: All her people [are] groaning, seeking bread; they have given their desirable things for food to bring back life. See, Yahweh, and look, for I have become worthless.
pieces: All her people groan as they search for bread; \q they trade their treasures for food to stay alive. \q Look, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, and take notice, for I am treated as worthless.

L.11: All her people groan, seeking bread; \q they have given their precious things for food, to bring back life. \q See, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, and look, for I have become worthless.

R.11: All her people groan as they look for bread. \q They give away their treasures for food so that they can stay alive. \q Zion cries: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, look at me! See how people despise me!

decisions.choice: seeking bread: the famine of the siege
decisions.reason: During the siege of Jerusalem the food ran out, and the famine was severe (2 Kings 25:3; Lamentations 2:11-12; 4:4-10).

decisions.choice: to bring back life: to keep themselves alive
decisions.reason: "To bring back the life (nefesh)" means to revive someone who is fainting from hunger or grief. The same phrase returns in verses 16 and 19.

decisions.choice: See, LORD: Zion speaks again, and goes on to the end
decisions.reason: As in verse 9, Zion breaks in with her own cry to the LORD. From here to the end of the chapter she speaks in the first person, apart from verse 17, where the poet's voice returns.

decisions.choice: worthless: of no account, despised
decisions.reason: The verb means to be light or cheap, of no value (Jeremiah 15:19). A related verb is used in verse 8: those who honored her now treat her as cheap.

decisions.choice: Zion cries:
decisions.reason: Readable marks the change of speaker, as in verse 9 (m3).

records.source: ל֣וֹא אֲלֵיכֶם֮ כָּל־עֹ֣בְרֵי דֶרֶךְ֒ הַבִּ֣יטוּ וּרְא֗וּ אִם־יֵ֤שׁ מַכְאוֹב֙ כְּמַכְאֹבִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֖ל לִ֑י אֲשֶׁר֙ הוֹגָ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה בְּי֖וֹם חֲר֥וֹן אַפּֽוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: Not to you, all passers-by [of the] road? Look and see if there is pain like my pain which has been dealt to me, which Yahweh has inflicted on [the] day of [the] burning of his anger.
pieces: Does it mean nothing to you, all you who travel this road? \q Look closely and see whether any pain is like my pain, the pain that was brought on me, \q which {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} laid on me on the day of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} blazing anger.

L.12: [Is it] nothing to you, all who pass along the road? \q Look and see if there is any pain like my pain, which was dealt out to me, \q which {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} inflicted on the day of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} burning anger.

R.12: Do you not care, all you people walking by? \q Look and see! Is there any pain like the pain that has been done to me? \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} made me suffer this on the day {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger burned hot.

decisions.choice: Not to you ...?: Is it nothing to you?
alternatives: May it not happen to you
Come, all you who pass by
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has only two words, "not to you", and their sense is unclear. Read as a question, Zion asks the travelers whether her suffering means nothing to them. They could also be a wish, "May it not happen to you", or, with a small change of letters, a call: "Come, all you who pass by." The question fits the call to look and see that follows.

decisions.choice: the day of his burning anger: the day of the LORD's judgment
decisions.reason: The prophets warned of a day when the LORD's anger would burn against sin (Isaiah 13:9, 13; Zephaniah 1:14-18; 2:2). Zion now says that day has come on her (2:1, 21-22).

decisions.choice: dealt out to me: done to me with severity
decisions.reason: The verb means to treat someone harshly, to deal out severe treatment. It returns in Zion's last prayer (verse 22) and in 2:20.

decisions.choice: Does it mean nothing to you (Balanced); Do you not care (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make the two short Hebrew words a full question, following the reading chosen in m1.

records.heading: Is any pain like my pain?

records.source: מִמָּר֛וֹם שָֽׁלַח־אֵ֥שׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַ֖י וַיִּרְדֶּ֑נָּה פָּרַ֨שׂ רֶ֤שֶׁת לְרַגְלַי֙ הֱשִׁיבַ֣נִי אָח֔וֹר נְתָנַ֨נִי֙ שֹֽׁמֵמָ֔ה כָּל־הַיּ֖וֹם דָּוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: From on high he sent fire into my bones, and it subdued them; he spread a net for my feet, he turned me backward; he has made me desolate, all the day faint.
pieces: From on high {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent fire into my bones, and it overpowered them; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spread a net to catch my feet and turned me back; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has left me devastated and sick all day long.

L.13: From on high {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent fire into my bones, and it prevailed over them; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spread a net for my feet, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} turned me back; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made me desolate, faint all the day.

R.13: From heaven {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent fire deep into my bones, and it overpowered me. \q He set a trap for my feet and made me turn back. \q He has left me ruined and weak all day long.

decisions.choice: and it prevailed over them: the fire overcame her bones
decisions.reason: The verb is most likely from a root meaning to rule over or subdue: the fire took hold of her bones. Its form could also mean that God "subdued" her. The ancient Greek translation reads "he brought it down", from a verb that looks almost the same.

decisions.choice: he spread a net for my feet: he caught her like a hunted animal
decisions.reason: Hunters spread nets to trap birds and animals. God says the same of Israel and of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah: "I will spread my net over him" (Ezekiel 12:13; Hosea 7:12).

decisions.choice: desolate, faint: ruined and sick
decisions.reason: "Desolate" is the word used of the deserted gates (verse 4) and the bereft children (verse 16). "Faint" means sick or unwell; it is used again of her heart in verse 22 and in 5:17.

decisions.choice: From heaven ... overpowered me
decisions.reason: Readable says "heaven" for "on high" and "me" for "them", the bones, since the fire is felt through her whole body.

records.source: נִשְׂקַד֩ עֹ֨ל פְּשָׁעַ֜י בְּיָד֗וֹ יִשְׂתָּֽרְג֛וּ עָל֥וּ עַל־צַוָּארִ֖י הִכְשִׁ֣יל כֹּחִ֑י נְתָנַ֣נִי אֲדֹנָ֔י בִּידֵ֖י לֹא־אוּכַ֥ל קֽוּם׃ס
records.gloss: Has been bound [the] yoke of my transgressions by his hand; they are knit together, they have come up on my neck; he has made my strength stumble; [the] Lord has given me into [the] hands of [those whom] not I am able to stand [against].
pieces: My rebellions are bound into a yoke by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand; \q they are lashed together and laid on my neck; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has drained my strength; \q the Lord has handed me over to those I cannot stand up to.

L.14: The yoke of my transgressions is bound fast by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hand; \q they are knit together, they have come up on my neck; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has made my strength fail; \q the Lord has given me into the hands of [those whom] I am not able to stand against.

R.14: The Lord has tied my sins together into a yoke and put it on my neck. \q He has taken away my strength. \q He has handed me over to enemies I cannot fight.

decisions.choice: is bound: is tied on like a yoke
alternatives: watch was kept over my transgressions
decisions.reason: The first word is found only here. It is best taken as "bound" or "fastened", like a yoke tied on with straps. The ancient Greek translation reads "a watch was kept over" my transgressions, from a Hebrew word that differs by one letter, which some prefer.

decisions.choice: the yoke on my neck: subjection to a foreign master
decisions.reason: A yoke on the neck is the picture of being made to serve. Jeremiah wore a yoke to show that the nations must serve the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:2, 8, 12; 28:14). Here her own sins, woven together by God's hand, have become that yoke.

decisions.choice: the Lord: God's title as master
decisions.reason: Here and twice in verse 15 Zion uses the title Adonai, "the Lord", which speaks of God as master and owner, instead of his name. It suits the picture of the yoke.

decisions.choice: rebellions (Balanced); sins (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "rebellions" and Readable "sins" for the word Literal renders "transgressions", as in verse 5.

decisions.choice: The Lord has tied ... He ... He
decisions.reason: Readable names the Lord in its first sentence, where the Hebrew says "his hand", and then says "He" for the rest of the verse.

records.source: סִלָּ֨ה כָל־אַבִּירַ֤י׀אֲדֹנָי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י קָרָ֥א עָלַ֛י מוֹעֵ֖ד לִשְׁבֹּ֣ר בַּחוּרָ֑י גַּ֚ת דָּרַ֣ךְ אֲדֹנָ֔י לִבְתוּלַ֖ת בַּת־יְהוּדָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: Has rejected all my mighty ones [the] Lord in my midst; he has called against me an appointed assembly to break my young men; [as] a winepress has trodden [the] Lord [the] virgin daughter of Judah.
pieces: The Lord has cast away all the warriors within my walls; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has summoned an assembly against me to crush my young men; \q the Lord has trampled Virgin Daughter Judah as grapes are trodden in a winepress.

L.15: The Lord has thrown aside all my mighty men in my midst; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has called an appointed assembly against me to crush my young men; \q the Lord has trodden the virgin daughter of Judah [as in] a winepress.

R.15: The Lord has rejected all the strong soldiers who defended me. \q He called an army together against me to crush my young men. \q The Lord has crushed the people of Judah like grapes in a winepress.

decisions.choice: has thrown aside: has rejected as worthless
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. It is used in Psalm 119:118 for God rejecting those who stray. Here God has set aside the city's warriors as if they counted for nothing.

decisions.choice: an appointed assembly: a gathering called for a set time, here an army
decisions.reason: The word (mo'ed) is the one used for the appointed feasts in verse 4. The festival crowds no longer come; instead God has called a gathering of a different kind, an enemy army.

decisions.choice: trodden like a winepress: crushed in judgment
decisions.reason: Grapes were trampled by foot in a stone vat. The prophets use the picture for God's judgment (Isaiah 63:2-3; Joel 4:13). "The virgin daughter of Judah" pictures the people of Judah as a young woman (compare Isaiah 37:22).

decisions.choice: an army ... the people of Judah
decisions.reason: Readable says "an army" for the appointed assembly (m2), and "the people of Judah" for "the virgin daughter of Judah" (m3).

decisions.choice: as grapes are trodden in a winepress
decisions.reason: Balanced spells out the picture of the winepress.

records.source: עַל־אֵ֣לֶּה׀אֲנִ֣י בוֹכִיָּ֗ה עֵינִ֤י׀עֵינִי֙ יֹ֣רְדָה מַּ֔יִם כִּֽי־רָחַ֥ק מִמֶּ֛נִּי מְנַחֵ֖ם מֵשִׁ֣יב נַפְשִׁ֑י הָי֤וּ בָנַי֙ שֽׁוֹמֵמִ֔ים כִּ֥י גָבַ֖ר אוֹיֵֽב׃ס
records.gloss: Over these I [am] weeping; my eye, my eye runs down [with] water; for far from me is a comforter, [one] bringing back my life; my children are desolate, for has prevailed [the] enemy.
pieces: For all this I weep; my eyes stream, stream with tears, \q for no one is near to comfort me, no one to revive my spirit; \q my children are left forlorn, for the enemy has won.

L.16: Over these things I weep; my eye, my eye runs down with water, \q for far from me is a comforter, one to bring back my life; \q my children are desolate, for the enemy has prevailed.

R.16: This is why I cry. Tears pour and pour from my eyes. \q No one is near to comfort me or give me strength again. \q My children are ruined, because the enemy has defeated me.

decisions.choice: my eye, my eye: the word is repeated
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text says "my eye" twice. The ancient Greek translation and some Hebrew manuscripts have it once. The repetition fits a cry of grief (compare 2 Samuel 19:1, "my son, my son") and is kept.

decisions.choice: my eye runs down with water: tears flow without stopping
decisions.reason: The same picture is used of tears that will not stop (3:48-49; Jeremiah 9:17; 13:17).

decisions.choice: one to bring back my life: someone to revive me
decisions.reason: As in verse 11, to bring back the life (nefesh) is to revive someone. Here the reviving would come from comfort. No such comforter is near.

decisions.choice: my eyes stream, stream with tears
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the repetition of the Hebrew by repeating the verb (m1).

records.source: פֵּֽרְשָׂ֨ה צִיּ֜וֹן בְּיָדֶ֗יהָ אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לָ֔הּ צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה לְיַעֲקֹ֖ב סְבִיבָ֣יו צָרָ֑יו הָיְתָ֧ה יְרוּשָׁלִַ֛ם לְנִדָּ֖ה בֵּינֵיהֶֽם׃ס
records.gloss: Spreads out Zion with her hands; there is not a comforter for her; has commanded Yahweh concerning Jacob [that] those around him [be] his foes; has become Jerusalem an impure thing among them.
pieces: Zion stretches out her hands, but no one comforts her; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has given orders against Jacob that his neighbors be his foes; \q Jerusalem has become something unclean among them.

L.17: Zion spreads out her hands; there is no one to comfort her; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has commanded concerning Jacob [that] those around him [be] his foes; \q Jerusalem has become an impure thing among them.

R.17: Zion reaches out her hands for help, but no one comforts her. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has commanded the nations around Jacob's people to be their enemies. \q Jerusalem has become like something unclean that they keep away from.

decisions.choice: Zion spreads out her hands: the poet speaks about Zion again
decisions.reason: For one verse Zion's own voice stops and the poet describes her from outside, calling her "Zion", "Jacob" and "Jerusalem". In verse 18 Zion speaks again in the first person. There is no other mark of the change.

decisions.choice: spreads out her hands: the gesture of someone pleading
decisions.reason: Hands stretched out were the posture of prayer or of begging for help (Isaiah 1:15; Jeremiah 4:31; Psalm 143:6). No one takes her hands.

decisions.choice: an impure thing: something shunned like the impurity of monthly bleeding
decisions.reason: The word (niddah) is the term in the law for the impurity of a woman's monthly bleeding, which kept her apart from others for seven days (Leviticus 15:19-24; 18:19). It came to be used of anything defiling that people keep away from (Ezekiel 36:17; Ezra 9:11). Jerusalem's neighbors now avoid her as unclean (compare verse 8).

decisions.choice: Jacob: the people of Israel, named after their ancestor
decisions.reason: Jacob is the people descended from him, here the people of Judah. Their neighbors are the nations around them, such as Edom, Moab and Ammon, who joined in their fall (Ezekiel 25:1-14; Obadiah 10-14).

decisions.choice: the nations around Jacob's people ... like something unclean that they keep away from
decisions.reason: Readable says that Jacob stands for the people (m4) and explains what being treated as unclean meant (m3).

records.source: צַדִּ֥יק ה֛וּא יְהוָ֖ה כִּ֣י פִ֣יהוּ מָרִ֑יתִי שִׁמְעוּ־נָ֣א כָל־הָֽעַמִּ֗ים וּרְאוּ֙ מַכְאֹבִ֔י בְּתוּלֹתַ֥י וּבַחוּרַ֖י הָלְכ֥וּ בַשֶּֽׁבִי׃ס
records.gloss: Righteous [is] he, Yahweh, for his mouth I have rebelled against; hear, please, all the peoples, and see my pain; my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is in the right, for I rebelled against {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} word. \q Listen, all you peoples, and look at my pain: \q my young women and my young men have gone into captivity.

L.18: Righteous [is] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, for I have rebelled against {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mouth; \q hear, please, all peoples, and see my pain; \q my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.

R.18: Zion cries: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has done what is right, because I refused to obey {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. \q Listen, all you nations, and see how I suffer. \q My young women and young men have been taken away as prisoners.

decisions.choice: I have rebelled: Zion speaks again
decisions.reason: After the poet's words in verse 17, Zion resumes in the first person and speaks to the end of the chapter.

decisions.choice: the LORD is righteous: he is in the right to judge her
decisions.reason: Zion admits that God has done her no wrong. The same confession is made in other prayers after judgment (Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:7, 14; compare Jeremiah 12:1). Her grief does not turn into an accusation against God.

decisions.choice: rebelled against his mouth: disobeyed what he commanded
decisions.reason: "His mouth" means what he spoke, his command (Numbers 20:24; 1 Samuel 12:14-15).

decisions.choice: all the peoples
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has "all peoples"; the reading tradition adds "the". The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: his word (Balanced); refused to obey him (Readable); young women
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "his mouth" means (m3), and they say "young women" for the virgins, as in verse 4.

decisions.choice: Zion cries:
decisions.reason: Readable marks that Zion speaks again after the poet's words in verse 17, as in verses 9 and 11 (m1).

records.source: קָרָ֤אתִי לַֽמְאַהֲבַי֙ הֵ֣מָּה רִמּ֔וּנִי כֹּהֲנַ֥י וּזְקֵנַ֖י בָּעִ֣יר גָּוָ֑עוּ כִּֽי־בִקְשׁ֥וּ אֹ֨כֶל֙ לָ֔מוֹ וְיָשִׁ֖יבוּ אֶת־נַפְשָֽׁם׃ס
records.gloss: I called to my lovers; they deceived me; my priests and my elders in the city perished, for they sought food for themselves and they would bring back their life.
pieces: I called to my lovers, but they let me down; \q my priests and my elders breathed their last in the city \q as they searched for food to keep themselves alive.

L.19: I called to my lovers; they deceived me; \q my priests and my elders perished in the city, \q while they sought food for themselves to bring back their life.

R.19: I called to the nations I had loved, but they tricked me. \q My priests and my leaders died in the city \q while they were looking for food to keep themselves alive.

decisions.choice: my lovers deceived me: her allies failed her
decisions.reason: As in verse 2, her lovers are the nations she relied on. When the Babylonians besieged the city, the help hoped for from Egypt came to nothing (Jeremiah 37:5-10).

decisions.choice: my priests and my elders: the city's leaders in worship and in government
decisions.reason: The elders were the heads of families and the leaders of the people (2:10; 5:12). Even they died of hunger in the siege.

decisions.choice: to bring back their life
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation adds "and they did not find it" at the end. The Hebrew does not have the words, but the sense is the same: they died while they searched.

decisions.choice: the nations I had loved ... my leaders
decisions.reason: Readable says who the lovers were (m1), and "leaders" for the elders.

records.source: רְאֵ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה כִּֽי־צַר־לִי֙ מֵעַ֣י חֳמַרְמָ֔רוּ נֶהְפַּ֤ךְ לִבִּי֙ בְּקִרְבִּ֔י כִּ֥י מָר֖וֹ מָרִ֑יתִי מִח֥וּץ שִׁכְּלָה־חֶ֖רֶב בַּבַּ֥יִת כַּמָּֽוֶת׃ס
records.gloss: See, Yahweh, for distress [is] to me; my inner parts are in turmoil; my heart is turned over within me, for rebelling I have rebelled; outside has bereaved [the] sword; in the house [it is] like death.
pieces: Look, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, how distressed I am! My stomach churns; \q my heart is overturned inside me, for I have rebelled so deeply. \q Out in the street the sword takes my children; indoors there is only death.

L.20: See, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, for I am in distress; my inner parts are in turmoil; \q my heart is turned over within me, for I have been very rebellious; \q outside the sword has bereaved; in the house [it is] like death.

R.20: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, see how troubled I am! I am sick with grief inside. \q My heart is broken within me, because I have rebelled so badly. \q Out in the streets people are killed by the sword. Inside the houses there is death.

decisions.choice: my inner parts are in turmoil: deep anguish felt in the body
decisions.reason: The inner parts are where grief and distress are felt (Jeremiah 4:19; Lamentations 2:11). The verb means to foam or ferment: her insides churn.

decisions.choice: my heart is turned over: she is overcome by remorse
decisions.reason: The heart is the inner self. To have it turned over within oneself is to be shaken by strong feeling (Hosea 11:8). Here it goes with her confession: "I have been very rebellious."

decisions.choice: rebelling I have rebelled: I have rebelled greatly
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for strength, as "sin" is in verse 8. It is the same verb as "I have rebelled" in verse 18.

decisions.choice: outside the sword, in the house death: the curse of the Song of Moses
decisions.reason: Moses' song warned, "Outside the sword will bereave, and in the rooms terror" (Deuteronomy 32:25). "Death" may mean plague, which killed people in their houses while the sword killed them in the streets (Jeremiah 14:18; 15:2).

decisions.choice: takes my children (Balanced); people are killed (Readable); My heart is broken (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb "bereave" means to take a parent's children from them. Balanced says this; Readable says plainly that people are killed. Readable also says "my heart is broken" for the heart turned over (m2).

records.source: שָׁמְע֞וּ כִּ֧י נֶאֱנָחָ֣ה אָ֗נִי אֵ֤ין מְנַחֵם֙ לִ֔י כָּל־אֹ֨יְבַ֜י שָׁמְע֤וּ רָֽעָתִי֙ שָׂ֔שׂוּ כִּ֥י אַתָּ֖ה עָשִׂ֑יתָ הֵבֵ֥אתָ יוֹם־קָרָ֖אתָ וְיִֽהְי֥וּ כָמֽוֹנִי׃ס
records.gloss: They heard that groaning [am] I; there is not a comforter for me; all my enemies heard of my trouble, they rejoiced that you have done [it]; you have brought [the] day you proclaimed, and let them be like me.
pieces: People have heard my groaning, with no one to comfort me. \q My enemies have all heard of my disaster and are glad that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have done this. \q Bring on the day {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} announced, and let them become as I am!

L.21: They have heard that I groan; there is no one to comfort me; \q all my enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have done [it]; \q bring the day {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have proclaimed, and let them be like me!

R.21: People have heard me groaning, but no one comforts me. \q All my enemies have heard about my trouble. They are happy that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} did this to me. \q Bring the day {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} promised, and let them suffer as I do!

decisions.choice: they heard: people heard
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject: people in general have heard her groaning, and it has moved no one to help. The ancient Greek translation reads "Hear!", a call like those in verses 12 and 18.

decisions.choice: bring the day: a plea, though the verb is past in form
alternatives: you have brought the day you announced
decisions.reason: The verb is in the form normally used for a completed act ("you have brought"). Followed by "let them be like me", it is best read as a plea that what God announced will surely happen. It may also be read as a statement: "you have brought the day you announced", meaning the day of judgment on Zion, with the wish for her enemies only in the last words.

decisions.choice: the day you proclaimed: the day of judgment on the nations
decisions.reason: The prophets announced that the cup of the LORD's anger would pass from Jerusalem to the nations around her (Jeremiah 25:15-29; Obadiah 15-16; Lamentations 4:21-22).

decisions.choice: my enemies are glad: neighbors who rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall
decisions.reason: Edom and others gloated over Judah on the day of its ruin (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 12; Ezekiel 25:3, 6).

decisions.choice: People (Balanced, Readable); done this to me (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "people" as the subject (m1); Readable says what God did.

records.source: תָּבֹ֨א כָל־רָעָתָ֤ם לְפָנֶ֨יךָ֙ וְעוֹלֵ֣ל לָ֔מוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר עוֹלַ֛לְתָּ לִ֖י עַ֣ל כָּל־פְּשָׁעָ֑י כִּֽי־רַבּ֥וֹת אַנְחֹתַ֖י וְלִבִּ֥י דַוָּֽי׃פ
records.gloss: Let come all their evil before you, and deal with them as you have dealt with me because of all my transgressions; for many [are] my groans, and my heart [is] faint.
pieces: Let all their wickedness come before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}; deal with them \q as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have dealt with me for all my rebellions, \q for my groans are many and my heart is sick.

L.22: Let all their evil come before {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and deal with them \q as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have dealt with me because of all my transgressions; \q for my groans are many, and my heart is faint.

R.22: Look at all the evil things they have done. \q Punish them as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have punished me for all my sins. \q I groan and groan, and my heart is weak.

decisions.choice: let their evil come before you: let it be brought to your notice for judgment
decisions.reason: To come before God is to be laid before the judge, like a case in court (Psalm 79:11; 109:14-15; Jeremiah 18:23).

decisions.choice: deal with them as you have dealt with me: a prayer for justice
decisions.reason: Zion does not take revenge herself but asks God to judge her enemies by the same measure he has used for her, as the law and the prayers of Israel leave vengeance to God (Deuteronomy 32:35; Psalm 137:7-8; Jeremiah 11:20; Lamentations 3:64-66). She does not deny her own guilt: she was judged "for all my transgressions".

decisions.choice: deal with: treat severely
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used in verse 12 ("dealt out to me"): to deal out hard treatment.

decisions.choice: faint: the alphabet ends
decisions.reason: The verse begins with taw, the last letter of the alphabet, and closes the poem. Its last words, a heart that is faint, echo verse 13.

decisions.choice: Look at ... Punish them as you have punished me
decisions.reason: Readable says what bringing their evil before God and dealing severely with them mean (m1, m3).

decisions.choice: rebellions (Balanced); sins (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 5.
